transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-11
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Jenna Park (Redwood AE), Marco Diaz (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (StellarHealth CTO), Tom Reynolds (Platform), Priya Patel (Security), Liam O'Connor (SRE)

Summary section (auto): quick run-through of org/project keys, demo of console policy UI, answering security questions; plan to send security pack and pricing spreadsheet; schedule POC.

00:00 Jenna Park: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll do a quick 45-ish minute demo then Q&A, Marco's gonna show the console and api patterns for org vs project keys
00:18 Marco Diaz: awesome, yes so at a high level Redwood supports two main key types, org keys which are essentially umbrella keys for billing and org-wide quotas, and project keys which map to individual teams or apps, those can have overrides, uh, override quotas and rate limits
00:35 Aisha Khan: quick question — can project keys be isolated from org metrics for compliance reasons? we need per-project retention and separate audit trails
00:50 Marco Diaz: yes you can enable per-key logging and retention, the console shows retention policies per project, and we also stream audit logs to your S3 or SIEM; there was a note in the security docs, link: https://app.redwood.ai/docs/security (note: auto transcript mangles links sometimes)
01:05 Priya Patel: and KMS? keys must be customer-managed for PHI use-cases
01:12 Marco Diaz: we support CMEK via AWS KMS and bring-your-own keys on private deployments, for hosted we integrate with your KMS using our control-plane tunnel when requested under an enterprise contract
01:38 Tom Reynolds: how do rate limits work — we have multiple teams hitting inference, some spiky traffic from mobile and some steady from backend batching
01:50 Marco Diaz: two layers: org-level bucket (global quota for your account) plus project-level buckets. We support both steady-rate and token-bucket bursting. So mobile spikes can consume project burst capacity up to configured burst size while the org cap prevents runaway costs
02:10 Jenna Park: I'll demo the console now, Marco will flip to the policy UI, you'll see where you set per-project egress tokens and per-minute QPS, and then you can set fallback policies to throttle or route to a cheaper model
02:28 Marco Diaz: (screen) alright, in the Console > Projects > preview-project, you can see API key, usage charts, then Policies > Rate limits. Here you can set RPS, token-per-minute, and daily quota. You can also attach a policy to a key so that key can't exceed X tokens per day
02:45 Priya Patel: does changing a policy retroactively affect running sessions? we need predictable behavior for ongoing calls
02:54 Marco Diaz: policy changes are applied at request-evaluation time; long-running streaming calls keep existing session until next token check — there are options to enforce immediate cutoffs but default is graceful degrade to avoid half-completed responses
03:10 Liam O'Connor: for the POC we need burst for 120 seconds and then strict throttle after, is that doable?
03:18 Marco Diaz: yes that's a burst-window config, you can set a short-term burst bucket with a decay to steady rate, the console has presets or you can use the API to set exact windows
03:32 Aisha Khan: what about multi-tenant models where multiple client orgs share the same project internally — can we create sub-projects or use tags?
03:45 Marco Diaz: you can create nested projects via the API and then assign project keys — current Console supports org->project hierarchy plus metadata tags. For stricter isolation you'd use separate projects with their own quotas and optionally dedicated capacity
04:02 Tom Reynolds: dedicated capacity would help predictability; how does Redwood route requests when dedicated is full? we can't afford failed requests during spikes
04:12 Marco Diaz: routing policies can be set to fallback to hosted instance or a lower-cost model. You can set canary and fallback models; also queueing and retry settings are configurable so you won't immediately get hard failures unless you configure hard reject
04:30 Priya Patel: audit logs — how long do you retain them and can we push to our own SIEM?
04:38 Marco Diaz: retention is configurable per project and org, default 90 days; you can forward to your S3 or Splunk/Datadog via our logging connector. For compliance you can set longer retention on private deployments
04:55 Jenna Park: quick note, for PHI we usually recommend Private or Dedicated with CMEK, but many customers start with hosted and then move to Private if they need full network isolation
05:12 Aisha Khan: any throttling at region level? we have EU data residency constraints
05:20 Marco Diaz: yes regions are enforced and you can pin projects to regions; rate limits are enforced per region + org quotas across regions if you want aggregated billing limits
05:34 Tom Reynolds: can we create rate-limit tiers per environment — i.e. staging vs prod — with the same project key family?
05:44 Marco Diaz: typical pattern is to create separate projects for staging and prod, but you can also attach environment tags and use policy overrides per key; we usually recommend separate project keys for clear billing separation
06:00 (screen) Marco shows API request examples
06:12 Marco Diaz: example curl: POST /v1/generate with header x-redwood-project-key: proj_xxx, and the service will evaluate the key’s policy and apply quotas; response includes x-redwood-throttle and x-redwood-rate-limit headers so your app can react
06:30 Jenna Park: we'll also include a sample SDK snippet for handling 429s and backoff. Most customers implement exponential backoff plus fallback strategies to a cached response or cheaper model
06:45 Aisha Khan: how do we measure per-customer cost? our finance team wants per-client chargebacks
06:52 Marco Diaz: you can tag requests with metadata, and usage reports can be exported daily with per-project and per-key granularity; project tags map to your cost centers
07:10 Priya Patel: anything around quotas for embeddings vs generation tokens? we have heavy embedding workloads that are cheaper but high volume
07:20 Marco Diaz: quotas are resource-type aware, you can set separate token quotas for generation and embedding units, embedding calls count against embedding quotas, not generative token quotas, and you can set quotas and alerts per resource type
07:38 Tom Reynolds: alerts — can we hook into PagerDuty for quota breaches?
07:42 Marco Diaz: yep webhook connectors to PagerDuty/Slack/email; and you can set thresholds like 80% daily usage to trigger warnings
07:54 (15m mark) Jenna Park: quick recap of what's been demoed — console policies, API headers, audit logs, CMEK options, dedicated fallback behaviours, and cost export. We'll open it up for deeper security questions
08:20 Priya Patel: encryption-at-rest fine, but we need to know exactly what metadata Redwood stores with requests and how long model caches persist — we don't want PHI in any long-lived KV cache
08:35 Marco Diaz: default behavior is ephemeral KV caches for low TTLs; you can opt out of caching per project and disable prefix caching. For hosted we don't persist request text beyond logs unless you opt into retention for evaluation; private deployments can be configured for no retention
09:00 Aisha Khan: curious about RBAC — can we have read-only for finance and admin for ops?
09:09 Marco Diaz: yes multi-role RBAC in Console: Owner/Admin/Developer/Read-only and you can scope roles to projects or org level and integrate with SSO/SAML for provisioning
09:28 Tom Reynolds: any rate limit exceptions for internal health-checks or infra calls? we need a small always-on allowance for heartbeats
09:35 Marco Diaz: yep you can create an internal system key class that has unlimited very small qps allowance or exempt certain IPs if on private/dedicated networks
09:50 (20m mark) Marco shows Policy JSON example
20:10 Marco Diaz: here's a policy snippet, again you can push via REST or terraform provider; note corp parser sometimes transcribes code incorrectly so we'll send the raw file after the call
20:30 Jenna Park: side note — when customers migrate to dedicated we typically provision a reserved pool and you can reserve burst capacity on top for predictable spikes; pricing has a compute baseline plus token usage
20:50 Aisha Khan: for pilot we'd want three projects: web-summarizer, mobile-cta, analytics. Can those be billed separately and have separate SLAs?
21:02 Marco Diaz: yes separate projects map to separate usage buckets and invoices can be broken out by project tags; SLA tiers are org-level but you can mix and match routing so mission-critical projects hit dedicated nodes first
21:20 Priya Patel: if we need additional controls around IP allowlists and network isolation, is that Private only?
21:28 Marco Diaz: network isolation (VPC peering, private control plane) is a Private deployment feature; Dedicated provides VLAN-ish isolation but not full VPC unless it's a Private offering
21:45 Tom Reynolds: what about rollout controls per key? say we roll a new model to 10% of traffic for project A only
21:53 Marco Diaz: canary rollouts are per-project; you can set percent traffic at the policy level and use rule-based routing to split by key or route by header metadata
22:10 Jenna Park: ok we'll open the floor for specific PII/PHI flow questions
22:22 Priya Patel: what exactly appears in the audit logs? request headers, key id, timestamps, model version?
22:30 Marco Diaz: logs include key id, request id, timestamp, model id, token counts, response latencies, and optionally anonymized prompts; we can include full prompts for projects that opt-in for evals but default is partial or hashed to protect PHI
22:50 Aisha Khan: that's good, can we redact patient names in logs automatically?
22:58 Marco Diaz: we have optional pre-ingest redaction pipelines you can enable; they run regex/ML redactors and can mask PII before it's written to logs
23:18 Liam O'Connor: do you have a recommended config for mobile spike protection?
23:24 Marco Diaz: yes pattern is short burst bucket per project (e.g., 1000 tokens over 60s) plus a global org cap and smart caching at edge. We'll share a template config
23:40 Jenna Park: I'm going to share the pricing/rate spreadsheet and security packet right after; Marco will add a sample policy and a terraform snippet
24:00 (mid-call) Aisha Khan: let's talk timeline — we want to run a 6-week POC starting late August if that's possible
24:12 Jenna Park: that's doable, we'll propose a pilot with dedicated reserved hours for two weeks then measure cost and latency, success criteria: under 250ms p95 for summaries and per-client cost below $0.003 per summary on average
24:30 Priya Patel: what about rollback and data deletion after pilot? we need guarantees for data purge
24:38 Marco Diaz: we provide deletion APIs and can schedule secure purge in private deployments; for hosted we can purge logs and disable retention but backups policies are separate — we'll include details in the security packet
25:02 Tom Reynolds: any limits on number of project keys? we might have 50+ internal apps
25:10 Marco Diaz: scale-wise no, you can create many project keys; we can help with org hygiene and naming via the API, and tag-based cost reports help manage that scale
25:28 (30m mark) Marco walks through Alerts & Usage dashboard
30:45 Marco Diaz: dashboards show per-key QPS, tokens/day, and cost; you can export CSVs or hook to BigQuery for analytics
31:05 Aisha Khan: can we set automated throttles based on spend thresholds?
31:12 Marco Diaz: yes spend-based policies are in the policy engine, you can enforce hard cutoffs when spend reaches X for the month and send alerts earlier
31:30 Jenna Park: any final security blocking items?
31:38 Priya Patel: need SOC2, encryption details, KMS diagrams, retention and purge flow — will review security doc after you send it
31:48 Marco Diaz: noted, sending full packet; also we'll include sample audit log exports and terraform snippets for policies
32:05 Aisha Khan: one ask — can you include an example where an org-level daily quota is enforced but a project has an exception for a short window? we want to see that behavior before POC
32:18 Marco Diaz: sure we'll create a small demo script you can run during POC to simulate exceptions and show enforcement in real-time
32:32 Jenna Park: great, we'll circle back on the commercials; any blockers from finance right now?
32:40 Aisha Khan: none, finance just wants per-project cost visibility which you said is supported
32:48 Liam O'Connor: last infra question — do you support ephemeral keys rotated automatically?
32:54 Marco Diaz: yes short-lived keys via our sessions API, you can issue ephemeral tokens with TTL and tie them to service accounts; works well for mobile and server-to-server flows
33:10 (40m mark) Marco: quick demo of terraform provider to create project + policy
40:30 Marco Diaz: terraform provider snippet — resource redwood_project { name = "web-summarizer" } resource redwood_policy { project = redwood_project.web-summarizer.id rules = [...] } (we'll send raw file later)
40:50 Tom Reynolds: will policy change logs be auditable? we need who changed what and when
40:58 Marco Diaz: yes policy changes are audited with user id and timestamp and stored in the audit log stream, you can set longer retention for policy events
41:12 Priya Patel: any penalties for overages on dedicated? we need clarity for procurement
41:20 Jenna Park: commercial typically has overage rates or auto-burst pricing; for pilots we can cap to avoid surprise charges; details will be in the proposal
41:36 Aisha Khan: ok let's confirm next steps and owners
41:42 Jenna Park: owners: Marco will send policy examples and terraform, Jenna will send pricing and get pilot proposal out, Aisha to confirm POC participants and timelines
42:00 (closing) Marco Diaz: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and the sample scripts, feel free to email security@redwood.ai if additional security questions come up
42:14 Aisha Khan: thanks all, good session
42:20 (call end)

Notes: transcript contains typical auto-transcription errors, speaker overlaps, and occasional mis-spellings. Links and code snippets to be attached to follow-up email.
